title: Materiality, Memory, and the Poetics of Everyday Life
bio:
Xixi Xu is a London-based multidisciplinary artist working across printmaking, painting, and mixed media. She holds an MA in Print from the Royal College of Art.
Before pursuing her postgraduate studies in London, Xu spent a decade running a barbecue restaurant in China. This experience continues to inform her artistic practice, grounding her exploration of memory, materiality, and everyday life.
Working with paint alongside unconventional materials such as wax, quartz sand, eggshells, and chilli powder, Xu creates layered surfaces that connect personal memory, lived environments, and inner emotional landscapes. Her practice investigates how materials can carry traces of experience, allowing abstraction to emerge through processes of accumulation, transformation, and tactile experimentation.

content.text: Prior to studying printmaking at the RCA, you ran a barbecue restaurant in China for ten years. Looking back, how does this lived experience inform your current working mindset and creative habits?

Running a barbecue restaurant for ten years taught me a great deal about
persistence, discipline, and the realities of everyday life. The work was busy and
repetitive, but it also taught me to pay attention to small details and to find meaning in
ordinary experiences.
At the same time, the restaurant became an unexpected source of curiosity for my
artistic practice. I became interested in bringing materials and experiences from that
environment into my work, and I enjoy the collision between things that might initially
seem completely unrelated. This has led me to experiment with materials such as
chilli powder, eggshells, and other everyday substances, allowing experiences from
my daily life to enter the studio in unexpected ways.
I believe that every stage of life matters and that each experience leaves something
behind. The ten years I spent running a restaurant were not separate from my journey
as an artist; they became part of the foundation that eventually brought me to London
to pursue my artistic practice. In this sense, my work continues to grow directly from
my lived experience, and I see the everyday as an important source of both material
and thought.
Your practice incorporates unconventional materials such as chilli powder, eggshells, quartz sand, and wax. What prompted you to bring these specific elements into your artistic work?

The materials I use often come directly from my lived experience, particularly from my
ten years of running a barbecue restaurant in China. They are materials that I
encountered repeatedly in everyday life, so bringing them into my work is also a way
of bringing those memories into the studio.
Chilli powder, for example, was something I used every day in the restaurant. It is
connected not only to food, but also to smell, colour, taste, and physical sensation.
These sensory qualities can trigger memories in a very immediate way, sometimes
before I am even consciously aware of them.
Eggshells were also part of the daily life of the restaurant. I began keeping them
because I became interested in their fragility and their connection to life. By bringing
something that would normally be discarded into my work, I feel that I am giving it
another life and allowing it to exist in a different form.
Quartz sand has another connection to the restaurant. Barbecue required charcoal,
and at the end of each working day, we would use earth and sand to extinguish the
charcoal fire. This repeated physical action became part of my memory of the place.
When I use sand in my work now, I am bringing a trace of that experience and of that
daily rhythm into the studio.
Wax interests me through its changing physical state. It can melt, harden, become
transparent or opaque, and retain traces of heat and touch. I am drawn to this ability
to change while also preserving traces of what has happened to it. In this sense, wax
connects closely to my interest in memory—something that can be held onto, but can
also shift and transform over time.
I don’t choose these materials simply because they are unusual. I choose them
because they carry a physical and emotional connection to my life. Through the
process of transforming them within the artwork, everyday experiences can become
part of a new visual and sensory language.
In your statement, you frequently address "materiality" and "transformation". During your actual making process, what role do the materials themselves play in your practice?

I do not try to completely control the materials. Instead, I allow them to flow and
respond naturally, accepting what happens rather than forcing them into a
predetermined result. For me, the material is not simply a tool; it is part of the process
and, in a sense, becomes a collaborator.
Wax, for example, can produce unexpected results as it melts, hardens, and
accumulates. I enjoy building layer upon layer, because the process reminds me of
life itself—there are moments that feel successful and others that may feel more
difficult or imperfect. I have learned to accept both. I see this coexistence of positive
and negative outcomes as part of the beauty of the process.
The eggshells often break during the making process, and rather than seeing this as a
problem, I respond to the broken form and allow it to influence what happens next.
Quartz sand mainly contributes weight and texture, while chilli powder can gradually
oxidise and change colour over time. I find this particularly interesting because it
gives the material a sense of life. As colour changes and begins to deteriorate, I can
also see a kind of beauty in that process of ageing and decline.
I therefore think of my practice as working with materials rather than simply
controlling them. I enjoy finding a balance within uncertainty. Quite often, a work ends
up very differently from what I initially imagined. This happens because I approach
the process through questioning, exploration, and enjoyment rather than trying to
reach a fixed result. When a work moves away from my original idea, it often allows
me to discover something new about my own practice and about myself.
As a multidisciplinary artist with a background in printmaking, how do the specific methodologies of printmaking carry over into your current mixed-media painting?

My background in printmaking continues to influence the way I approach painting,
particularly through my understanding of layering, repetition, and the accumulation of
marks. I enjoy building an image gradually, allowing each layer to respond to what
came before it rather than trying to establish the entire composition from the
beginning.

Printmaking also taught me to accept a certain degree of uncertainty. The final result
of a print is not always completely predictable; processes such as transferring,
pressing, layering, and removing an image can produce unexpected marks and
relationships. I find this openness very important in my current mixed-media painting
practice.
Although I now work primarily with painting and mixed media, I still think about the
surface almost as a printmaking plate—something that can be built up, altered,
partially erased, and transformed through successive layers. This way of working
allows traces of previous decisions to remain visible within the final image.
In this sense, printmaking has become less about a specific technique and more
about a way of thinking. It has taught me to work through accumulation and
transformation, while remaining open to results that I could not have fully anticipated.
Looking at your work Untitled (2025), we see an interplay of various shapes and layered surfaces. Could you talk about the initial starting point and the evolution of its composition?

Untitled (2025) did not begin with a fixed image or a clearly defined composition. I
started with a theme and a feeling that I carried with me, rather than a specific visual
plan. As the work developed, I allowed myself to listen to my intuition and respond to
what was happening on the surface. I gradually added forms, colours, and layers,
allowing each decision to influence the next.
The composition was built through continuous layering and accumulation rather than
by repeatedly starting over. I don’t see each new layer as correcting the previous one;
instead, it becomes part of the history of the surface. As a result, the final
composition is quite different from what I initially imagined, but I feel that it became
stronger through this process of discovery.
The work is also connected to my personal pursuit of freedom and to the Chinese
mythological figure of the Thousand-Armed Guanyin. The many arms of Guanyin have
stayed with me as an image of protection, compassion, and strength. For me, this
connection is also personal: I see my journey from China to London and my pursuit of
an artistic life as something that has been accompanied by a sense of protection and
support.
In this work, the reference to Guanyin becomes a way of expressing gratitude as well
as freedom. It reflects my feeling that I have been fortunate to have the opportunity to
come to London and pursue the life and artistic practice I wanted. Rather than
illustrating the myth directly, I wanted to allow its presence to exist within the
abstraction as part of my own experience and memory.
Drift of Matter (2025) possesses a distinctive sense of dynamic energy. How did you approach the relationship between color, movement, and mark-making while creating this piece?

Drift of Matter (2025) began from a very intuitive and spontaneous moment of
painting. I was in a relaxed state and wanted to allow myself to paint freely, without
thinking too much about where the work should go. At the beginning, I had an image
in my mind of an endless blue—something between the vastness of the ocean and the
depth of the night sky. I wanted to capture the feeling of joy and freedom associated
with that sense of openness, rather than represent a particular landscape.
The physical movement of my body became an important part of the painting process.
I started with quick and expansive gestures, allowing the marks to develop through
movement rather than planning each one in advance. Most of the surface was built
through painting, while some areas were scraped back, creating changes in texture
and allowing earlier layers to remain visible.
As the painting developed, colour, gesture, and emotion became closely connected.
The blue creates a sense of openness and depth, while the energetic marks give the
surface a sense of rhythm and movement. I was interested in allowing the painting to
remain open and alive, rather than bringing it towards a fixed image.
For me, Drift of Matter is ultimately about the feeling of letting go. The painting grew
out of a moment when I allowed myself to follow the process completely, and the final
work became a record of that freedom and enjoyment.
While your work leans toward abstraction, recognizable silhouettes and natural forms occasionally appear. How do you view the presence of these visual elements within your compositions?

Although my work leans towards abstraction, I intentionally allow recognisable forms
and silhouettes to emerge within the compositions. I prefer to express these forms in
a subtle and suggestive way rather than presenting them as clearly defined images. I
enjoy the moment when a form feels familiar, but remains open to interpretation.
These elements are closely connected to my everyday surroundings and personal
memories. I often think of them as fragments of memory entering the painting. They
may suggest a natural form, a body, or another familiar presence, but I do not want to
determine exactly what the viewer should see. For me, the ambiguity is important
because it allows each viewer to bring their own memories and experiences into the
work.
I also see abstraction and figuration as closely connected rather than separate. In my
practice, abstraction often grows out of something recognisable. A form may begin
with a reference to the physical world, but through layering, transformation, and the
process of painting, it gradually becomes less defined and moves towards
abstraction.
In this sense, the recognisable elements are not simply images within the
composition. They are fragments of memory—traces of places, experiences, and

things I have encountered—which remain somewhere between recognition and
uncertainty.
You note that your work explores the intersection between memory and environment. How have shifts in space and environment (such as moving from China to London) influenced your artistic practice?

Moving from China to London has had a profound influence on both my personal life
and my artistic practice. I came to London on my own, leaving my parents, friends,
and the familiar environment of home behind. That sense of distance and solitude
was one of the biggest changes for me.
China is still home for me, and I see it as the place where my roots are. London,
however, represents a place where I have chosen to pursue my artistic ambitions and
a different sense of freedom. Although there are moments of loneliness, being away
from everything familiar has also allowed me to focus more deeply on my practice.
London has also opened up a new visual environment for me, particularly through its
exhibitions, galleries, and the experience of moving through the city.
Living away from home has made me think about the past differently. Distance has
given me a kind of wider perspective on my previous experiences, allowing me to look
back at people, places, and memories with a different understanding. I often feel that
every stage of my life has mattered, and that each experience continues to contribute
to who I am now.
At the same time, London itself has become part of my work. I visit exhibitions, travel
around the city, and often use painting as a way of recording my impressions of the
places I encounter. My practice therefore moves between the memory of China and
my experience of London. I don’t see these as separate worlds; the past becomes part
of how I understand the present. Even my earlier works have become a way of looking
back at my own development and recognising new ideas and changes in my practice.
For me, pursuing art in London is also connected to a broader idea of freedom. I
believe that life is not only about making a living or earning money, but also about
having the courage to pursue the things that matter to you. Coming to London was
my decision to follow that part of myself.
Your works exhibit rich physical textures and tactile surfaces. What kind of tactile quality or sensory atmosphere do you aim to evoke through these surfaces?

Texture is an essential part of my practice because, for me, it is closely connected to
memory and bodily experience. I am drawn to surfaces that feel rough, complex, and
physically present. I want the surface to create a sense that it could almost be
touched, even though the viewer can only experience it visually.

The textures in my work come directly from my lived experiences and from the
materials I encounter in everyday life. Different materials bring different physical
qualities to the work: the fragility of eggshell, the grain and weight of quartz sand, the
softness and changing state of wax, and the fine, powdery quality of chilli powder. I
am interested in allowing these qualities to remain present rather than completely
transforming them into something else.
For me, texture is therefore more than a visual effect. It carries the memory of
physical contact and everyday experience. When these different materials come
together on the surface, they create a layered sensory experience in which memory
becomes something physical. I hope the viewer can sense this complexity and feel an
impulse to look more closely, perhaps even imagining what the surface might feel like
to touch.
Building on your ongoing exploration of memory and material, what new artistic avenues or media are you currently interested in testing next?

I am interested in continuing to explore the relationship between painting and
photography, as well as finding ways to move beyond the traditional two-dimensional
surface and bring painting into space. I am curious about how an image can exist
between photography, painting, and physical materials, and how these different forms
might influence one another.
I also want to continue exploring materials that have personal connections to my life,
including wax, eggshells, chilli powder, and sand. My family’s barbecue restaurant is
still operating in China, so this part of my life remains present and continues to
provide me with materials, memories, and possibilities for further experimentation. I
am interested in seeing how these everyday experiences might develop into new
forms rather than simply repeating what I have done before.
I would also like to explore the relationship between China, London, travel, and the
memories that accumulate through moving between different places. Photography
may become an important part of this process, allowing me to record places and
moments that can later enter my paintings or other forms of work. I am increasingly
interested in allowing painting to move into a more spatial and immersive context.
At the same time, I feel that my next stage of development may actually involve doing
less. Much of my current practice has developed through layering, accumulation, and
material experimentation, but I am becoming increasingly interested in simplicity. I
want to explore how fewer elements, quieter surfaces, and more space might
communicate a sense of calm and stillness. For me, this is not about abandoning the
complexity of my earlier work, but about gradually finding a quieter way of expressing
what I have experienced.
